awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: AI-Powered Prostate MRI Analysis Software
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact / commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is to potentially improve the accuracy, consistency, and efficiency of prostate cancer diagnosis using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Today, MRI scans used in prostate cancer screening can vary significantly depending on the machine and manufacturer, which makes it challenging for radiologists and software to provide consistent assessments. This project aims to create a software system that standardizes these images and provides accurate, editable 3D outlines of the prostate to support diagnostic decisions. The technology will help ensure that patients, regardless of where or how they are scanned, receive the same high-quality analysis. By reducing unnecessary imaging, streamlining radiologist workflows, and enabling more consistent evaluations, this innovation has the potential to improve early detection and reduce disparities in care. If successful, the solution will become an essential part of the prostate imaging workflow, supporting a variety of downstream clinical tools and improving access to equitable and efficient prostate cancer care.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will develop a style-encoding generative adversarial network (GAN) to harmonize prostate MRI images from different scanner vendors and field strengths while preserving anatomical detail. A transformer-based UNETR segmentation model will then produce precise binary masks of the prostate and voxel-level uncertainty maps. The architecture includes a segmentation-aware loss function that ensures harmonized images maintain diagnostic utility when passed through a frozen segmentation model. Phase I will evaluate this pipeline using a diverse, multi-vendor prostate MRI dataset. Key performance indicators will include segmentation accuracy using the Dice similarity coefficient and Hausdorff distance, anatomical fidelity measured by structural similarity (SSIM), and radiologist editing time. Successful completion of this project will establish the technical feasibility of a scanner-agnostic, confidence-aware segmentation tool capable of supporting real-time, human-in-the-loop clinical workflows.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in men, and magnetic resonance imaging or MRI, has become central to how it is diagnosed. An MRI scan helps physicians decide the next steps in treating the patient's cancer and whether intervention is needed. But interpreting a prostate MRI is slow and demanding work. Radiologists manually trace the outline of the prostate, take measurements, compare several different image types, and prepare structured reports using software that is often fragmented and cumbersome. The result is delays for patients, heavy workload for physicians, improper diagnosis and uneven quality of care across hospitals, particularly outside major academic centers.

This NSF SBIR Phase I project supported the development of segMedix, an AI software built to make prostate MRI analysis faster, more consistent, and easier to integrate into clinical care. The project addressed a problem at the core of medical imaging AI: the same prostate, scanned on two different MRI machines, can produce images that look noticeably different. Brightness, contrast, and texture all vary with the scanner manufacturer and the image protocols used. AI models trained on one type of scanner often perform poorly on another, a serious obstacle to deploying these tools in real hospitals, which use a wide range of equipment.

SegMedix built and tested an AI model that automatically identifies the prostate on MRI images. The model was trained and evaluated using over 1700 scans with six major scanner manufacturers such as Siemens and Philips. On average, the model’s outlines strongly overlapped with expert radiologist outlines, with a peak overlap score of 93.6%, better than the project's original technical target (Figure 1). Critically, when the model was tested on scans from manufacturers that were not used in training, performance held up at about 90%. This kind of external validation is the strongest test of whether a medical AI tool will actually work in the real world, on patients and machines it has never seen before.

The project also showed that better AI is not just a matter of building a bigger model. SegMedix tested techniques for standardizing MRI images before they reach the AI, so that scans from different manufacturers look more alike to the software. This image standardization meaningfully improved performance on the more difficult scanner types, suggesting that the path to reliable medical AI runs through both data and algorithms (Figure 2).

Beyond the AI model itself, segMedix built workflow tools that address the repetitive, time-consuming steps radiologists face during prostate MRI interpretation. Today, radiologists often have to move between disconnected systems to review images, trace the prostate, calculate measurements, prepare reports, and transfer information to urologists for treatment planning. SegMedix brings these steps into one platform, allowing radiologists to review the MRI, use AI-assisted prostate segmentation, edit the result, calculate key measurements, generate structured outputs, and export information for downstream clinical use within a unified workflow. Achieving this required technical development beyond the segmentation model. SegMedix built software that converts AI-generated prostate outlines into editable three-dimensional models, allowing physicians to review, adjust, and approve the result rather than blindly accept a fully automated output. SegMedix also developed standardized export capabilities so that prostate outlines could be transferred in medical imaging formats used by prostate biopsy systems. These technical workflow components help connect radiology and urology workflows that often operate separately.

An additional outcome of the project was a custom annotation platform developed with the radiology team at University Hospitals (Figure 3). This platform allowed radiologists and radiology fellows to produce expert-reviewed prostate outlines on 500 MRI studies, a substantial labeled dataset that is reusable for future research. The platform also gave clinicians hands-on experience contributing to a medical AI project and gave segMedix a much clearer picture of how radiology work actually happens.

The broader impact of this work is its potential to bring high-quality prostate MRI analysis to more patients and clinics. Roughly 333,830 men are diagnosed with prostate cancer in the United States each year, and the American Cancer Society states about 1 in 44 men will die of prostate cancer. and the quality of their MRI interpretation varies considerably depending on where they happen to live. By reducing repetitive manual work, standardizing parts of the MRI analysis workflow, and connecting radiology to downstream procedures, tools like this can help shorten the time between scan and diagnosis, support more consistent care across community and academic hospitals, and turn routine imaging into structured data that can be preserved, reviewed, and built upon by future research.

Over the course of Phase I, the project produced a validated AI segmentation model tested across multiple scanner types, a labeled dataset of over 1700 expert-reviewed prostate MRI studies, a reusable clinical annotation platform, three dimensional review tools for radiologists, and interoperability with prostate biopsy systems used in urology clinics.

  • AI prostate segmentation accuracy across MRI scanner manufacturers. Each line shows how closely segMedix's outlines matched radiologist outlines on validation scans from one manufacturer, across training epochs. The model reached a peak Dice score of 0.936, with five of six vendors above 0.90.
